analysis: Charles Codman (ME/MA, 1800-1842) at $1,000-1,500. Codman is the founding figure of Maine landscape painting -- a Portland artist working in the 1820s and 30s, and the earliest significant painter the state produced. He died in 1842, so this is unambiguously antique and unambiguously Maine: the rarest combination in the sale.
problems: Out of band, but only just at the low end -- $1,000 hammer is $1,320 all-in. This is the lot where I would most seriously consider stretching on criteria grounds, because a genuine Codman is the single best fit to 'true antique' and 'Maine' simultaneously. Verify the attribution carefully; Codman is copied and misattributed. Four photographs.
patience: Very low. Codman does not come round often and almost never inside four figures.

analysis: Eastman Johnson (MA/ME, 1824-1906) at $3,000-5,000 with eight photographs. Johnson was born in Lovell, Maine and is one of the major American painters of the 19th century -- a founder of the Metropolitan Museum. Genuinely antique, genuinely Maine-born.
problems: Three to five times the ceiling. At this level the attribution needs to be solid; Johnson is extensively copied and his drawings and sketches vary enormously in quality. Worth seeing at preview as the best American picture in the sale.

analysis: Carroll Sargent Tyson Jr. (ME/PA, 1877-1956) at $3,000-5,000, with a second at 2192 for $2,000-3,000. Tyson painted Mount Desert extensively and is a properly collected Maine coastal name.
problems: Out of band. Only two photographs for a four-figure lot. 2192 is the cheaper of the pair but still well past the ceiling.

analysis: The second Carroll Tyson at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Thomas Cole (1801-1848) at $5,000-7,000. Cole founded the Hudson River School and is one of the most important American painters there has ever been -- a genuine Cole is a museum object worth six or seven figures.
problems: Which is exactly why a $5,000-7,000 estimate should be read as a warning rather than an opportunity. At that price this is either a small sketch, a work with attribution problems, or not by him. The catalogue offers only the name and dates with no 'attributed to' qualifier, which is a strong claim it does not support. Far out of band regardless.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, and treat the attribution with real scepticism.

analysis: Frederic Remington (1861-1909) at $5,000-7,000, catalogued with no qualifier. Remington paintings are seven-figure objects; even his drawings run well into five.
problems: Same warning as the Cole. A $5,000 Remington is not a Remington painting -- it may be a print, a study of uncertain status, or wrong. Note lot 3178 in Day 3 is catalogued 'AFTER Remington', which shows the house does use the qualifier when it means it. Three photographs only.

analysis: Attributed to Theodore Robinson (1852-1896) at $20,000-30,000 -- the most expensive lot in the sale. Robinson was the leading American Impressionist of the first generation, a close associate of Monet at Giverny.
problems: 'Attributed to' is doing enormous work at this price. Per the standing principles that is an argument, not a fact, and at $20,000-30,000 you would want a catalogue raisonne reference or an expert opinion. Far out of band.

analysis: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot (1796-1875) at $20,000-30,000, catalogued with no qualifier. Corot is one of the most forged painters in history -- the standing joke is that he painted 3,000 pictures of which 10,000 are in America.
problems: At this price and with that reputation, documentation is everything and the catalogue supplies none. Far out of band. Recorded as the joint most expensive lot and the one carrying the greatest attribution risk.

analysis: Pierre-Auguste Renoir at $10,000-15,000, no qualifier. Note the catalogue gives his dates as 1841-1914; he died in 1919.
problems: A genuine Renoir oil is a seven-figure object, so at $10,000-15,000 this must be a drawing, a print, or an attribution the house cannot stand behind. The wrong death date does not inspire confidence. Far out of band.

analysis: Attributed to Jean-Leon Gerome (1824-1904) at $10,000-15,000. Gerome's Orientalist canvases make seven figures at the top of the market.
problems: 'Attributed to' again. Far out of band and the attribution unsupported in the catalogue.

analysis: Sir Peter Lely (1618-1680) at $3,000-5,000 with ten photographs -- the most thoroughly documented picture in Day 2. Lely was principal painter to Charles II and ran the largest studio in Restoration England.
problems: That studio is the problem: Lely's output was overwhelmingly produced by assistants to a formula, and 'Lely' in the trade usually means studio or circle rather than the master's hand. Out of band at three to five times the ceiling. The ten photographs at least let you judge the quality of the handling.

analysis: 'Manner of Anthony Van Dyck' at $3,000-5,000. The catalogue is honest -- 'manner of' is the weakest of all attribution formulas, weaker even than 'circle of' or 'follower of'.
problems: Out of band, and 'manner of' means the house is saying only that it looks like Van Dyck. Price it as an anonymous period portrait, which is a long way below $3,000.

analysis: A 17th-century English Civil War history painting at $1,500-2,500. Catalogued to the century, so among the oldest paintings in the sale, and a specific historical subject.
problems: Out of band. Anonymous. Seventeenth-century canvases invariably carry relining, old restoration and substantial overpaint -- five photographs will not show how much.

analysis: A portrait attributed to the circle of John Gordon Watson PRSA (1788-1864) at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band. 'Circle of' plus 'attributed to' is a doubly hedged formula -- it means the house thinks it resembles the work of people around an artist. Price accordingly.

analysis: A portrait of John Wilmot, 2nd Earl of Rochester, at $2,000-3,000. Rochester was the notorious Restoration poet and libertine, so the sitter carries genuine literary interest.
problems: Out of band, and no date or artist given -- portraits of Rochester were copied throughout the 18th and 19th centuries from the Huysmans prototype. Establish whether this is period or a later copy.

analysis: William Shayer Sr. (UK, 1787/8-1879) at $1,000-2,000. A properly documented English rustic-genre painter, unambiguously antique.
problems: Out of band at the top, though the low end is close. Shayer's market has softened considerably along with the rest of Victorian genre. Four photographs.

analysis: Anton Mauve (Netherlands, 1838-1888) at $1,000-1,500. Mauve was a leading Hague School painter and Van Gogh's cousin by marriage and first teacher, so the name is significant.
problems: Out of band, just. Mauve is also widely copied and his loose grey-toned manner is easy to imitate. Bidding already at $550. Six photographs.

analysis: Attributed to Gustave de Breanski (1856-1898), 'The Fishing Fleet', at $2,000-3,000. The de Breanski family produced several painters and their coastal and Highland scenes sell steadily.
problems: Out of band. 'Attributed to' with a family of similarly-named painters is a recipe for confusion -- Gustave is the least documented of them.

analysis: Francesco Lazzaro Guardi (1712-1793) at $2,000-3,000, no qualifier. A genuine Guardi view of Venice is a six or seven-figure picture.
problems: So a $2,000-3,000 estimate means this is not one -- it will be a studio work, a follower's picture, or a later Venetian view in his manner. Out of band regardless. Another case of a headline name at an estimate that contradicts the attribution.

analysis: 'In the mannor of Giovanni Ghisolfi' at $2,000-3,000 -- an architectural capriccio with ruins.
problems: Out of band, and 'in the manner of' is the weakest attribution formula. The catalogue also misspells 'manner'. Price as anonymous.

analysis: Pieter Barranti, Grand Tour era Florence, after Antonio Canova, at $1,000-1,500. Grand Tour marbles and bronzes after Canova were made for travellers and are genuine period objects even though the composition is borrowed.
problems: Out of band. 'After Canova' means a copy per the standing principles, though here the copying is the historical point rather than a deception.

analysis: Attributed to William Allen Wall (MA, 1801-1885) at $3,000-5,000. Wall was New Bedford's principal painter and documented the whaling town in its prime, which ties directly to the Day 2 whaling material.
problems: Out of band, and 'attributed to' per the standing principles. If firm, this would be an important New Bedford picture; as an attribution it is an argument.

analysis: Mary Blood Mellen (MA/NH, 1819-1886) at $1,000-2,000. Mellen was Fitz Henry Lane's only student and collaborator, and her luminist coastal scenes have risen sharply as scholarship has recovered her from Lane's shadow.
problems: Out of band at the top, close at the low end. Mellen and Lane worked so closely that attribution between them is genuinely contested -- which cuts both ways. Four photographs. Of the out-of-band American pictures this is among the more interesting.

analysis: Attributed to Martin Johnson Heade (1819-1904) at $1,000-1,500 with eight photographs. Heade's marsh scenes and hummingbird pictures are major American Luminism.
problems: Out of band, just. 'Attributed to' at an estimate this low relative to Heade's real market means the house has no confidence in it. A genuine Heade is six figures. Price as anonymous 19th-century American landscape.

analysis: Attributed to Thomas Sully (1783-1872) at $3,000-5,000. Sully was the leading American portraitist of the early 19th century.
problems: Out of band and attributed. Sully ran a busy studio and his portraits were copied by his own family; 'attributed to Sully' covers a wide range of realities.

analysis: 'In the manner of Alfred Jacob Miller' (1810-1874) at $10,000-20,000. Miller's Western scenes documenting the fur trade are important American pictures.
problems: Far out of band, and 'in the manner of' at a five-figure estimate is a striking combination -- the house is asking $10,000-20,000 for a picture it will not attribute. Approach with scepticism.

analysis: William Matthew Prior (1806-1873) and Sturtevant Hamblin (1816-1884) at $10,000-20,000. Prior and Hamblin ran the most important American folk-portrait workshop of the mid-19th century, and Prior worked in Bath and Portland, Maine before moving to Boston -- a genuine Maine connection.
problems: Far out of band at ten to twenty times the ceiling. Prior-Hamblin portraits are also attributed largely on style, since the workshop rarely signed. The most important American folk picture in the sale and comprehensively unaffordable.

analysis: A folk art portrait of two siblings at $2,500-3,500. Double child portraits are the most sought-after format in American folk painting.
problems: Out of band. Anonymous, and folk portraits are extensively faked because the market rewards them. Three photographs.

analysis: A circa-1810 pair of naive watercolour portraits of a brother and sister, Pitt family of Philadelphia, at $1,000-1,500. Dated, identified to a family, and a matched pair -- unusually well documented for folk material.
problems: Out of band, just. Watercolour folk portraits fade badly; check against the mat edge. Three photographs.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, but the documentation here is better than most folk lots.

analysis: A memorial portrait of a young man, circa 1850, at $1,000-2,000. Memorial or posthumous portraits are a distinct and rather affecting American genre.
problems: Out of band. Anonymous. Three photographs.

analysis: A pair of mid-19th-century portraits at $1,500-2,500. Pairs are worth more than singles because they were made and hung as pairs.
problems: Out of band, anonymous.

analysis: A portrait of George Comfort Kellogg (CT, 1788-1847) at $1,500-2,500, paired with his wife Clarissa at 2245. Named, dated sitters with a Connecticut family history and both halves of the pair present.
problems: Out of band. Sold as separate lots, which risks splitting a pair that has hung together for two centuries -- if you wanted them you would need both, doubling the cost.

analysis: The companion portrait of Clarissa Brown Kellogg (1794-1867) at $1,500-2,500.
problems: Out of band, and the same splitting problem as 2244.

analysis: A portrait of a wealthy Federal period American gentleman at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Out of band, just. Anonymous. Three photographs.

analysis: A circa-1845 portrait of a young lady at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Out of band. Anonymous, and only two photographs.

analysis: A portrait of a New England gentleman, circa 1810, at $3,000-5,000 -- the most expensive anonymous portrait in the sale.
problems: Far out of band. That estimate for an unattributed sitter and unattributed artist implies the house believes it is by someone identifiable; nothing in the entry says who.

analysis: A circa-1810 portrait of a girl in a Regency dress at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band, anonymous, only two photographs for a four-figure lot.

analysis: A portrait of Maria de' Medici, Queen of France (1575-1642), at $3,000-5,000. The sitter's dates are given; the painting's are not.
problems: Out of band, and the distinction matters -- royal portraits were copied for centuries. Three photographs.

analysis: An early 19th-century Italian portrait of a gentleman, possibly Filippo Re, at $2,000-3,000 with six photographs.
problems: Out of band. The identification carries a question mark in the catalogue itself.

analysis: An 18th-century Italian harbour scene, unsigned, at $5,000-10,000. Catalogued to the century, and harbour capricci in the Vernet and Guardi tradition are handsome pictures.
problems: Far out of band. The $5,000-10,000 spread is very wide, which signals real uncertainty about what it is.

analysis: A set of ten late 18th-century Neoclassical oil paintings of musicians at $1,000-1,500 -- roughly $120 a picture for genuinely 18th-century oils, which is remarkable value in principle.
problems: Out of band as a lot, though only just. Ten small decorative panels were probably made as an overdoor or furniture scheme, so they are ornament rather than pictures -- and you would be committing to hanging ten of them. Six photographs.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band, but the per-picture arithmetic is worth noting.

analysis: Albert E. Downs (MA, 1856-1923) at $1,000-1,500. Died in 1923, so unambiguously antique.
problems: Out of band, just. Minor name. Five photographs.

analysis: An H. Tasker portrait of the USS Maine at $1,200-1,500. The Maine's destruction in Havana in 1898 started the Spanish-American War, and the ship's name gives this a spurious but real appeal to a Maine collector.
problems: Out of band. 'H. Tasker' is effectively an unidentified signature. The ship is named for the state but has no other Maine connection. Five photographs.

analysis: Brian Coole (MA/UK, 1939- ) at $4,000-6,000. A living marine painter with a strong commercial following for detailed ship portraits.
problems: Far out of band and a living artist, so no discount and no antique claim. Three photographs.

analysis: Montague Dawson (UK, 1890-1973) at $5,000-7,000. Dawson is the most commercially successful marine painter of the 20th century and his clipper-ship pictures are instantly recognisable.
problems: Far out of band. Dawson is also heavily faked and his market has softened from its 1980s peak. Modern, so no antique claim.

analysis: Emil Fuchs (1866-1929) at $3,000-4,000. Note the current bid is listed as $5,000 -- above the high estimate, which is unusual and suggests either strong interest or a data anomaly worth verifying against the live page.
problems: Out of band. Fuchs was a society portraitist and sculptor with a modest modern market.

analysis: Eliphalet Fraser Andrews (1835-1915) at $5,000-7,000. Died in 1915, so unambiguously antique. Andrews painted official portraits including a well-known Martha Washington for the White House.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: John George Brown (1831-1913) at $1,500-2,000 with eight photographs. Brown's bootblacks and newsboys were among the most popular American pictures of their day.
problems: Out of band. His market has fallen a long way as sentimental genre went out of fashion, though the best examples still sell.

analysis: George Inness (1825-1894) at $2,000-3,000, no qualifier. Inness is a major American landscape painter whose best work makes six and seven figures.
problems: Out of band, and the same warning as Cole and Remington -- a $2,000-3,000 Inness is not a mature Inness landscape. Inness is also among the most forged American painters. Four photographs.

analysis: Amedee Joullin (MA/CA, 1862-1917) at $2,000-3,000. Died in 1917 so unambiguously antique; a California painter known for Native American subjects.
problems: Out of band and wrong coast.

analysis: William Trost Richards (1833-1905) at $1,500-2,500. Richards was a superb marine watercolourist and a leading American Pre-Raphaelite; his coastal studies are genuinely fine.
problems: Out of band. Five photographs. Of the out-of-band 19th-century American marine pictures this and the Bricher at 2229 are the two I would most want to see at preview.

analysis: Alfred Thompson Bricher (1837-1908) at $2,000-3,000 with seven photographs. Bricher painted the New England coast -- including Maine -- and his luminist beach and headland scenes are properly collected.
problems: Out of band. Bricher's watercolours are considerably cheaper than his oils; establish which this is.

analysis: Frederick Judd Waugh (1861-1940) at $8,000-12,000 -- the most expensive marine painting in the sale. Waugh was the pre-eminent American painter of open-sea surf and won the Popular Prize at the Carnegie five times.
problems: Far out of band. Six photographs.

analysis: Edward Henry Potthast (1857-1927) at $3,000-5,000. Potthast's beach scenes with children are among the most saleable American Impressionist pictures.
problems: Out of band. Potthast is also heavily faked precisely because the subject sells.

analysis: Lemuel Maynard Wiles (1826-1905) at $1,200-1,500. Died in 1905, so unambiguously antique. A Hudson River School follower.
problems: Out of band, just. Five photographs.

analysis: Guy Carleton Wiggins (1883-1962) at $1,000-1,500. Wiggins's snowy New York street scenes are instantly recognisable and consistently saleable.
problems: Out of band, just. He was extremely prolific and repeated the same Fifth Avenue motif for decades, so supply is deep. Also widely faked.

analysis: William Jurian Kaula (MA, 1871-1953) at $1,000-1,500. A New England landscape painter of the Boston school with a steady market.
problems: Out of band, just. Five photographs.

analysis: Harry Chase (1853-1889 or 1899) at $3,000-5,000. A well-regarded American marine painter of the late 19th century.
problems: Out of band. Note the catalogue's four-country attribution string is unusually long, which sometimes indicates the entry was assembled from a biographical database rather than from the picture.

analysis: Howard Hall Darnell (PA/ME, 1858-1939) at $1,000-1,500 -- one of three Darnells in Day 2 (2267, 2269, 2270) plus 1134 in Day 1. Four lots by one artist across two days.
problems: Out of band, and four lots means no scarcity whatsoever. If any of the four stalls near the ceiling it becomes interesting; otherwise the market will find its own level.

analysis: Second Day 2 Darnell at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Same as 2267.

analysis: Third Day 2 Darnell at $1,000-1,500, the last of the four in the sale.
problems: Same as 2267. Being the last of four is the best position if you wanted one.

analysis: Paul Emile Pissarro (1884-1972) at $3,000-5,000. The youngest son of Camille Pissarro, painting in a broadly Impressionist manner well into the 20th century.
problems: Out of band. The Pissarro name carries a premium that the son's own work does not really justify -- a familiar pattern with artistic dynasties.

analysis: Jean Carolus (Belgium, 1814-1897) at $5,000-7,000 with six photographs. Carolus painted highly finished Belgian genre interiors that sold well in his lifetime.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: Jozef Israels (Netherlands, 1824-1911) at $800-1,200. Israels was the leading painter of the Hague School and a major 19th-century figure.
problems: Only just inside the band at the low end -- $800 hammer is $1,056 all-in. But a genuine Israels oil is worth many multiples of that, so at this estimate it will be a drawing, a print, or an attribution the house cannot support. Three photographs. Treat a cheap major name as a red flag first.

analysis: Cornelia Loring Brooks (1874-1970) at $5,000-7,000 with six photographs.
problems: Far out of band. A very high estimate for an artist with a thin public record -- worth understanding what the house knows that the market does not.

analysis: Attributed to Charles-Francois Daubigny at $1,000-1,500. Note the catalogue gives his dates as 1870-1878, which is nonsense -- Daubigny lived 1817-1878. Another dates error.
problems: Out of band, 'attributed to', and the dates in the entry are wrong. Daubigny is also among the most forged Barbizon painters. Five photographs.

analysis: Fernand Cian (Italy, 1889-1954) at $1,000-1,500 with seven photographs.
problems: Out of band, just. Minor Italian name; the catalogue's parenthetical alternative spelling suggests uncertainty about the identity.

analysis: Ernst Adolf Meissner (Germany/Italy, 1837-1902) at $1,000-2,000. Died in 1902 so unambiguously antique.
problems: Out of band. Note this classified as Maine-associated only because 'Meissner' matches the Leo Meissner the brief names as a Monhegan wood engraver -- a different artist entirely, and a good example of why the automatic tagging needs the hand check.
